about: The golden fixture for device_link: approving a new device from one you already
have: the two-digit number a person picks, and the QR text the specification
reserves and no client uses.
The third table beside rules.json (what the GROUP policy decides) and
credentials.json (what the IDENTITY layer decides about a leaf); this one pins
the pure functions in mls/core/src/device_link.rs, which are product code on
every client rather than a protocol decision inside a group, and a fifth call
beside them - keyPackageIdentity - which is not a pure function and belongs here
anyway, because it is the other half of the same feature.
mls/core/src/device_link.rs is the reading guide and mls/core/src/fixture.rs is
the door a replay calls - the SAME door the other two tables go through, which is
why every case names its kind.
WHY ANY OF THIS EXISTS, in one paragraph, because a replay that does not know
this cannot tell a good change from a bad one. What an approving phone signs, and
seals the account key to, is a PUBLIC KEY it was handed over the network, and the
server is the thing that handed it over. A server that swapped that key would
collect a genuine signature over a key it holds itself, and every check in this
file would pass while checking the wrong key correctly. So the key crosses once
through the person, as a two-digit number both devices derive (commitment, number) from both keys and a fresh nonce
from each side, exchanged commit-then-reveal: the approver commits to its nonce
before the new device draws its own, and reveals it only after. A server in the
middle then matches one time in a hundred per exchange, and a failed exchange
leaves a number on the new device that is not among the approver's three.
"Per exchange" holds only because the new device releases ONE nonce per
pairing (waiterStep): the first exchange it answers binds the pairing to that
approver, that approver's key and that commitment; the same three continue it;
any other commitment or key from that approver ends the pairing, which the
device says was interrupted, and the person starts again by hand; and any other
approver is never answered. Without it a server, which knows the new device's
number before it reveals, could restart unseen until the numbers matched.
waiterStep/a-restart-after-a-shown-number-is-interrupted is that row.
THE APPROVER'S RULE (approverStep) is the mirror. The approver posts ONE
commitment per prompt, for the waiting row's key as it read it. The first read
that lists a device nonce under it FIXES that nonce before the reveal is posted;
a reveal whose post failed is sent again only over exactly the fixed key,
commitment and nonce; any change after that ends the prompt as interrupted. An
approver that took its number over whatever nonce a later read listed would
hand a server its nonce first and the choice of the other second.
approverStep/a-failed-reveal-then-another-device-nonce-is-interrupted is that
row. The approver also signs its commitment over the waiting device's id and key
(signCommitment, domain peachy-device-link-commit-v2), and the waiting device
answers only an exchange whose signature holds (verifyCommitment).
number/nonce-does-not-open-the-commitment is the row that holds the order, and
number/identical-keys the one that stops a device being compared with itself.
THE OTHER DIRECTION. Everything above tells the APPROVER that the key it lets
in is the key in the person's hand. The new device needs the converse: that the
account key it is handed comes from a device the person holds, and not from one
the server runs and lists as an approver. So the approver shows a second number
(approverNumber: the same five inputs under the domain
peachy-device-link-approver-v1) that the person picks on the new device. The
account-key side of this is in account-store.json (boxAcceptHybrid). qr and
qrMatches pin the QR text the specification reserves; no client uses it.
KEY MATERIAL IS SYNTHESISED, NEVER REAL, exactly as in credentials.json. Every
input here is either a repeated byte written out as hex, or a value DERIVED from
one by the implementation itself:
1111..11  Ada's phone, the APPROVING device's 32-byte Ed25519 seed
d04ab2..  its public half - signing_key_public_key(1111..11), not a typed key
4444..44  a second seed, for the wrong-approver case
d75979..  its public half, the approver who did not sign
2222..22  the new laptop's published signing key
3333..33  Bo's phone's signing key
aaaa..aa, bbbb..bb  stand-in public keys for the number; 5555.., 6666.. nonces
6f1c2a9e-..  a stand-in device row id for the QR code
Nothing here is, or could be mistaken for, a key any Peachy environment holds.
A public key in a `number` case is only ever hashed, and a `signingKeyHex` is only
ever message bytes, so neither has to be a curve point; an `approverKeyHex` does,
and the two that are real ones are derived above rather than written by hand.
WHERE THE APPROVED KEY COMES FROM, which is the keyPackageIdentity half. An
approval is a signature over a device id and a signing key; before adding that
device's leaf, an adder has to know that the key package it is about to commit
carries the SAME key the approval named. Taking the pair from the directory
response would give a server the last word: it could answer with a truthful
(deviceId, signingKey) for the check and a key package holding a different key,
and the leaf that landed would be one nobody approved, with every signature in
the exchange verifying. So the pair is read out of the key package's own bytes
(Client::key_package_identity), and keyPackageIdentity/the-directory-lied is the
row where that difference is visible. Its cases carry a nowUnix and a trust list
because the reader's clock and its issuer keys are what turn the same bytes into
an acceptance, an unknown_kid or an expired - and a producedAtUnix where the
PRODUCING device needs a different clock from the reading one, which is the only
way an expired-credential row can be written at all.
EVERY BYTE STRING CROSSES AS LOWER-CASE HEX, no prefix, in both directions. Hex
and not base64 because half this table is about LENGTHS - a 31-byte key, a
63-byte signature - and hex is the encoding whose length a reader can count.
A case carries EITHER an `expect` (the verdict object the door must return) or an
`expectError` (a substring the refusal must contain). The second kind is not
decoration: a signing key of the wrong length and an empty device id are refusals
and NOT verdicts, and a replay that turned either into a `valid: false` would be
the exact blur this fixture exists to prevent. `verify` is the one call that
cannot fail - a malformed key, a wrong length and a bad signature all come back
as valid:false, because a caller that could tell them apart would be holding an
oracle.
Replayed by every client, each through its own door and none of them
re-deciding anything: mls/core/tests/device_link_fixture.rs (Rust),
mls/wasm/tests/node/device-link.test.mjs (JavaScript, through the wasm binding),
mls/swift/Tests/PeachyMLSTests/DeviceLinkFixtureTests.swift and
the Android binding's `DeviceLinkFixtureTest` (not in this repository) (the last two
through peachy_mls_fixture_evaluate_case in the C ABI).
The expected values were produced by running the Rust implementation, never by
hand. Ed25519 is deterministic (RFC 8032), so a golden signature is a real
assertion about the bytes and not a shape check.
THE ACCOUNT IDENTITY KEY (docs/identity.md 'The account identity key').
Three more pure calls, from mls/core/src/account_identity.rs: accountIdentity
derives an account's public identity key from its 32-byte account key (a1a1..a1
is Ada's, a2a2..a2 another account's), signAccountDevice is that key vouching for
one device key, and verifyAccountDevice checks it - false, never an error, for
every way it fails. Every keyPackageIdentity mint carries its actor's account key,
because a key package from a device its account never let in is refused as
not_approved, which the last case shows.

domains.note: The ASCII domain separators, spelled out so a reader of a Swift or Kotlin port can check them against the hex below without a Rust toolchain. 'peachy-device-approval-v1' is 7065616368792d6465766963652d617070726f76616c2d7631, 'peachy-device-link-commit-v1' is 7065616368792d6465766963652d6c696e6b2d636f6d6d69742d7631 and 'peachy-device-link-v2' is 7065616368792d6465766963652d6c696e6b2d7632. 'peachy-device-link-approver-v1' is 7065616368792d6465766963652d6c696e6b2d617070726f7665722d7631. 'peachy-device-link-kem-v1' is 7065616368792d6465766963652d6c696e6b2d6b656d2d7631.

cases.why: The exact bytes an approving device signs, written out so that a port can be checked byte for byte without running anything: the ASCII domain, 0x00, the device id in ASCII, 0x00, then the 32-byte key. Both the id and the key are in there because either alone would be forgeable into something else - a signature over the key alone replays onto any device row holding that key, and one over the id alone vouches for whatever key the server later decides that row holds.

A second id and a second key, so the statement is visibly a function of both rather than a constant with a key stuck on the end. Its middle segment differs from the case above in length as well as in content, which is what the 0x00 separators are for.

31 bytes. A refusal and NOT a verdict: a caller handing over something that is not a device key has made a mistake, and a statement built over 31 bytes would be signed happily and verify against nothing. The message names the field and the size it wanted, so a client can say which argument was wrong.
cases.expectError: a signing_key must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: 33 bytes, the other side of the same boundary. Written out because a length check spelled `< 32` passes this one, and a fixture that only ever tested the short side could not tell the two spellings apart.
cases.expectError: a signing_key must be exactly 32 bytes, got 33

cases.why: An empty id would produce a statement of domain, 0x00, 0x00, key - a perfectly good byte string that vouches for a key attached to no device row at all. Refused rather than signed.
cases.expectError: a device_id must not be empty

cases.why: Ada's phone signs the laptop. Ed25519 is deterministic, so this signature is a golden value and not a shape check: a port that hashed the statement first, or reordered the domain, produces 64 perfectly valid-looking bytes that are not these.
The same approving seed over a different device, so the pair proves the signature moves with the statement. Its verdict is the input of verify/second-round-trip below.

A 31-byte seed. Refused with the same sentence mls/core/src/identity.rs uses for signing_key_public_key, because it is the same seed and a caller that got two different messages for one mistake would go looking for two bugs.
cases.expectError: a device signing key seed must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: The statement's refusals reach through sign rather than being re-checked there. A port that validated the seed and then built the statement inline would sign this one.
cases.expectError: a device_id must not be empty

cases.why: The ordinary case, and the only one that proves the others are about something: sign/ada-approves-the-laptop's signature, under the public half of the seed that made it. A verifier that refused everything would pass every other verify case in this table.
sign/ada-approves-bo-phone's signature, checked the same way. Two round trips and not one, because a verifier that compared against a single hard-coded statement would pass the first.
The round-trip signature with the low bit of its first byte flipped. The cheapest possible forgery, and the one a verifier that had stopped calling Ed25519 at all would accept.

A real signature over the laptop, presented as an approval of Ada's phone. This is the replay the device id is IN the statement to stop: without it, one approval would vouch for every row that ever held this key.

The other half of the same idea: the right device id, the wrong key. This is the swap the whole feature is about, and it is the one the cryptography CAN catch - the one it cannot is the server swapping the key before the phone ever signed, which is what the link code is for.
A genuine signature, a genuine statement, and the public key of a device that did not sign it (the public half of 4444..44). Somebody else's approval is not yours.

63 bytes: the round-trip signature with its last byte cut off. FALSE and not an error, and that is the decision this row exists to pin - a caller that could tell a truncated signature from a wrong one would be holding an oracle, and every call site would then have to decide for itself which failures are safe to read as no.
65 bytes: the same signature with a trailing zero. The other side of the boundary, and the shape a verifier that read the first 64 bytes and ignored the rest would accept.
31 bytes of approver key. False, on the same terms as the truncated signature: a malformed key is a question about the shape of a secret nobody offered, and there is exactly one safe answer to it.

A signing key that statement/ and sign/ both REFUSE arrives here as false instead. The asymmetry is the point: building a statement over nonsense is a caller mistake, and being asked whether nonsense was approved has an answer.
The same asymmetry for the id. Refused when signing, answered when verifying.

Step one: the approver publishes SHA-256 of its nonce under its own domain and nothing else. The nonce stays on the approver until the new device has published its own; this row pins the bytes so four clients commit to the same thing.
31 bytes. Refused rather than hashed: every nonce in this exchange is exactly 32 bytes from the platform's CSPRNG, and a short one is a caller bug, not a weaker commitment to accept.
cases.expectError: a approver_nonce must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: The ordinary number: the new device's key (aaaa..), the approver's key (bbbb..), the approver's commitment, the new device's nonce (5555..) and the approver's revealed nonce (6666..). Two digits, which is what a person can read off one screen and find among three on another.

THE SAME TWO KEYS IN THE OTHER ROLES. The number is not symmetric: the new device's key is always first, because each side knows which role it plays. A port that sorted the keys would pass the row above and fail this one.
Only the new device's nonce changed. It is what the approver cannot know when it commits, which is the half of the guarantee that stops a server choosing the approver's number.
Only the approver's nonce (and so its commitment) changed. It is what the new device cannot know when it publishes its nonce, which is the half that stops a server choosing the new device's number.
Ada's phone's actual public key as the approver and the laptop's as the new device, so the table is not made only of keys whose bytes are all equal.

A device nonce chosen for exactly one property: its number starts with a zero. The padding is load-bearing - '07' and '7' are the same number to the hash and two different things to a person looking for it among three.

REFUSED, and this is the row the whole exchange rests on. The approver's nonce must open the commitment the new device saw BEFORE it drew its own nonce; a number over a nonce that was never committed is a number a server could have picked after seeing the other side.
REFUSED. A number over one key in both roles is a perfectly good hash, and it would render as a MATCH on the screen asking whether these are two different machines.
cases.expectError: a device cannot be compared with itself

cases.why: 31 bytes, refused rather than hashed, and the refusal names the argument.
cases.expectError: a new_device_key must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: 33 bytes on the other side's nonce, and it names device_nonce - a port that checked one argument twice would pass the row above and fail this one.
cases.expectError: a device_nonce must be exactly 32 bytes, got 33

cases.why: The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/ordinary, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. An independent draw from the first number.

The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/the-keys-swapped, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. An independent draw from the first number.

The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/a-different-device-nonce, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. An independent draw from the first number.

The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/a-different-approver-nonce, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. An independent draw from the first number.

The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/a-real-derived-public-key, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. An independent draw from the first number.

The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/leading-zero-is-kept, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. An independent draw from the first number.

The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/nonce-does-not-open-the-commitment, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. It refuses what that row refuses.
The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/identical-keys, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. It refuses what that row refuses.
cases.expectError: a device cannot be compared with itself

cases.why: The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/new-device-key-one-byte-short, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. It refuses what that row refuses.
cases.expectError: a new_device_key must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: The approver's number, the one the person picks on the new device: the same five inputs as number/device-nonce-one-byte-long, under the domain peachy-device-link-approver-v1. It refuses what that row refuses.
cases.expectError: a device_nonce must be exactly 32 bytes, got 33

cases.why: What the new device's QR code carries: the prefix, its device row id, a slash, and its whole 32-byte key in lower-case hex. The whole key and not a fingerprint, because a fingerprint is something a server could grind and the key is not. The link secret rides after the key, in lower-case hex: the new device drew it for this pairing and keeps it, and it reaches the approver only through the camera.
Refused: the slash is the separator, and an id containing one would make the text ambiguous.
31 bytes, refused rather than encoded.
cases.expectError: a signing_key must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: The link secret is 32 bytes like the key. A shorter one is a caller bug, never a shorter code.
cases.expectError: a link_secret must be exactly 32 bytes, got 31

cases.why: The approver scanned the waiting device's own code, and the row it was handed carries the same id and key: approve.
A scanner's trailing newline is not a different code.
THE ROW THIS EXISTS FOR. The id matches and the key does not: the server handed the approver a row carrying a key of its own. Never approve.
Another waiting device's code: not this one.
Only the exact text matches; a re-encoded code is not one Peachy drew.
A QR code from anywhere else is false, never an error.
A waiting row whose key is not 32 bytes matches nothing.
A code that carries the key and no link secret is not a code this build draws. Matching it would let an approver seal a box the new device has no secret for.
A secret of 31 bytes is not a secret this build draws.
The secret is lower-case hex, as the code is drawn. Anything else is some other text.
Nothing may follow the secret.
Any well-formed secret matches; the approver seals with the one it read.

Ada's account identity key, derived from her 32-byte account key: seed = HKDF-SHA256(account key, info 'peachy account identity v1', empty salt). The key every peer pins for Ada. Every device that holds the account key derives the same one.
31 bytes is not an account key.
cases.expectError: an account_key must be exactly 32 bytes

cases.why: Ada's account vouching for her laptop: Ed25519 by the derived identity key over 'peachy-account-device-v1' || 0x00 || device_key. Deterministic, so the bytes are pinned.
The signature above, checked against Ada's identity key.
The same signature checked against a different account's identity key. False: an account signs for its own devices only.
Ada's signature for the laptop, offered for a different device key. False.
63 bytes. False, not an error: every way a certificate fails is the same answer.

Ada's account revoking her laptop: Ed25519 by the derived identity key over 'peachy-device-revocation-v1' || 0x00 || device_key. What RevokeDevice carries, and what a peer checks before it removes the laptop's leaf on more than the server's word. Deterministic, so the bytes are pinned.
31 bytes is not a device key.
cases.expectError: a device_key must be exactly 32 bytes

cases.why: The revocation above, checked against Ada's identity key.
The same revocation checked against a different account's identity key. False: an account revokes its own devices only, and the server holds no account's key.
The account's certificate for the laptop, offered as its revocation. False: the domains differ, so the signature that let a device in can never be replayed to take it out.

The other half of an approval, and the reason it is checkable at all. An approval says 'this device id with this signing key'; this is where those two values come from. They are read out of the key package's OWN bytes, by a client that trusts a set of issuer keys and believes a particular time - never taken from the directory response that carried the package. The issuer seed is credentials.json's 07x32 stand-in for the Peachy server, so the two tables cannot drift on what a pdc1 is; the laptop's device seed is 33x32 and its public half is the deviceKeyHex below.

The same package, with the device id the directory claimed for it. matchesClaim is true, which is the ordinary case and the one worth pinning beside the next row: a check that could only ever answer false would be no check.

THE ROW THIS DOOR EXISTS FOR. The very same package, served with somebody else's device id attached. A client that took the id from the server would verify Ada's approval of her phone and then add her laptop's leaf - the approval checks out, every signature verifies, and the leaf that lands is one nobody approved. matchesClaim is false, and it is false because the package was read and the server was not.

A VERDICT and not an error, exactly as on a roster. The credential expired 800 seconds before the reader's clock; producedAtUnix puts the producing device back at issue time, because a device cannot build a key package against a credential its own clock says is already dead - which is why two clocks are needed to write this row at all. A caller gets a name and a number and can say 'that device's credential expired' rather than 'no'.

The package is perfectly well formed and its credential is perfectly well signed - by 99x32, which this reader has never heard of. This is the shape a forged key package takes when whoever made it could not reach the server's signing key, and the answer has to be a refusal that names the reason rather than a leaf quietly admitted.

The other end of the window, a day ahead of the reader and well past any tolerated skew. Worth its own row beside the expired one because the two are one comparison written twice, and a port that got the sign wrong passes one and fails the other.

REFUSED, not rejected, and the distinction is the whole design. A rejection means 'this is a key package and I will not believe it'; four bytes of nonsense are not a key package at all, and folding the two together would let a caller report 'that device's credential is bad' about something that was never a credential.

An empty body is the shape a truncated or dropped directory response takes, and it must reach the caller as a failure rather than as an empty identity that compares equal to nothing and is therefore quietly 'not a match'.
A case-author mistake, refused by name. A keyPackageIdentity case says where its bytes come from - a mint or a literal - and one that says neither would otherwise read a verdict off nothing.

Not a verdict either. A client validates its own credential before it will open at all, so a reader trusting no issuer cannot exist to read anything - and a row that returned 'unknown_kid' here would be describing a client that never existed rather than a package that was refused.

The clock is an input and never the machine's: every expiry verdict in this table is an answer about a particular moment, and a case that left it out would pass today and start failing on a date nobody chose.

A key package from a device whose credential carries no account certificate - the device a server could add on its own. Every reader refuses it as not_approved and adds nobody. The fixture forges the package: an honest client refuses to make one.

A PAIRING THAT HAS ANSWERED NOTHING answers the first commitment it sees, and that answer binds it: to this approver, the key the device list gives for it (bbbb..) and this commitment (the one 6666.. opens).
The same pairing with the three binding fields present but empty, which is how a client with nothing bound crosses an ABI. Empty means none, and only all three empty does.

The exchange this pairing answered, read again: the same approver, key and commitment. The device sends the SAME nonce again if the row lost it, and derives the number, over the bound key, once the approver reveals.

THE ROW THAT HOLDS THE ODDS. The approver this pairing answered now shows a different commitment (the one 7777.. opens): the exchange was started over. A server knows the number the waiting device would show before it reveals anything, so a device that answered every fresh commitment would let it restart, silently, until the numbers matched. One nonce per pairing: the pairing is over, the device shows no number, says it was interrupted, and answers nothing until the person starts again by hand.

The same approver and commitment under a different key (cccc..). The approver's key is an input to the number that the server supplies; read again after the reveal it would be the one input the server could still choose with all the others known. Bound at the answer, a change ends the pairing.

Another approver's exchange while this pairing is bound: never answered, and it ends nothing. A port that answered it would release a second nonce in one pairing, which is the restart by another name.
A bound approver with no key or commitment beside it. Half a binding must never read as no binding, which would answer again.
A bound key and commitment with no approver id: the same mistake from the other side.
An offered commitment of 31 bytes: a refusal, never a verdict. The caller skips the exchange, binding and answering nothing.
An offered exchange with an empty approver id.

The approver signs its commitment together with the waiting device's id and key, under the domain peachy-device-link-commit-v2. Ed25519 is deterministic, so the statement and the signature are golden values. The waiting device answers only an exchange whose signature holds, so a server cannot stand in as this approver toward it.
31 bytes of commitment: a caller bug, refused, and the refusal names it.
No waiting device named: refused when signing.
The ordinary case: signCommitment/ada-commits-for-the-laptop's signature under the public half of 1111..11, over the waiting device's own id and key. The waiting device answers this exchange.

THE SUBSTITUTION. The approver signed the commitment for the key it was shown; a waiting device holding a different key (3333..) finds the signature does not hold for its own key, and answers nothing. A server that swapped the key toward the approver cannot reuse the approver's commitment toward the real device.
The same signature presented to a different waiting row: false.
A commitment the approver did not sign (the one 7777.. opens), under its real signature: false. A server cannot restart the exchange in the approver's name.

A genuine signature under the key of a device that did not make it (the public half of 4444..44): false. The key the waiting device checks against comes from its own device list, from an approved, unrevoked, certified row.
Ada's approval signature over the laptop (sign/ada-approves-the-laptop), presented as a commitment signature: false. The two statements have different domains, so one can never read as the other.
63 bytes: false, never an error.
A prompt just opened for the waiting row (key aaaa..) and nothing of ours is on it: post the commitment (the one 6666.. opens) with its signature.

Another commitment under our approver id (the one 7777.. opens; a stale read, another window) while nothing is fixed: post OUR commitment again, never a fresh one. One commitment per prompt, and nothing has been revealed.
Our commitment, no device nonce yet: wait.
The first device nonce (5555..) under our commitment. The caller FIXES it, then posts the reveal. Everything after is judged against it.
The reveal post failed; the row still lists the same key, commitment and device nonce we fixed: post the same reveal again.

THE ROW THAT HOLDS THE ODDS. The reveal post failed, so the server holds our nonce (6666..) and could search offline for a device nonce that makes both numbers match. The next read lists one (5757..) with our reveal stored. An approver that derived its number over it would show the server's choice. It is not the nonce we fixed: interrupted, no number, approval closed.
The same substitution before our reveal is stored: interrupted, and no second reveal over it.
Our reveal is listed over the device nonce we fixed: show the number, derived over the prompt's key and the FIXED nonce.
The waiting row now carries another key (bbbb..) than the one the prompt was opened for and the commitment signature covers: interrupted.
A device nonce was fixed and the reveal sent, and the row now lists no exchange of ours: interrupted, never a fresh commitment.
A device nonce was fixed, and the row now lists another commitment under our id: interrupted.
A stored approver nonce that does not open our commitment (7777..): interrupted.
Our reveal is listed though this prompt never fixed a device nonce: this prompt did not send it. Interrupted.
The caller's own fixed nonce is 31 bytes: a bug in the caller's state, refused rather than read as nothing fixed.
The caller's pending key is 31 bytes: refused.

The waiting device draws a fresh 32-byte seed for each pairing and posts the X-Wing (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) public key it derives: 1216 bytes. The derivation is deterministic, so the key is a golden value. The approver seals the account key to it as well as to the device's X25519 key, so a recording of the pairing does not open once X25519 falls.
Another seed, another key.
31 bytes of seed: a caller bug, refused.

The waiting device (seed 3333..) signs its link key together with its row's id, the approver's commitment and its own nonce, under the domain peachy-device-link-kem-v1: the domain, 0x00, the id in ASCII, 0x00, the 32-byte commitment, the 32-byte nonce, then the 1216-byte link key. Its signing key is the one the two-digit number is derived over, so a link key the approver accepts is the one this device posted.
1215 bytes of link key: refused when signing, and the refusal names it.
